text:
Distinguish semantic equivalence—no observable difference on any admissible input—from inactivity on sampled inputs: mutation unreachable, untriggered, or producing no state change. Survival on 32 users cannot establish equivalence. Record reachability, internal-state infection, propagation to a prespecified score/ranking/recommendation output, and detector alarm separately; an infected state need not change recommendations, and changed recommendations need not trigger detection. Define numerical tolerances beforehand. [Mutation-testing framework](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~rjust/publ/medusa_icst_2019.pdf).

Recommended reporting per fault class/category: attempted, valid, reached, infected, output-changing and detected counts. Report activation coverage as infected/valid cases; conditional sensitivity as alarms/infected cases, or alarms/output-changing cases if the detector targets recommendation failures—explicitly name the estimand. Also report alarms/all valid injected cases as end-to-end yield; do not silently discard inactive cases. A zero eligible denominator means undefined sensitivity. False-alarm rate uses clean controls; alarms on behaviorally unchanged mutant cases require a separate label. Traditional mutation score instead counts distinct killed mutants over distinct valid, nonequivalent mutants, never user cases. These denominator recommendations apply the [reach–infect–propagate distinction](https://www.tuwien.at/doc/res/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/property-based-mutation-testing.pdf).

With ≤32 users/category, report counts and category/class results. For uncertainty conditional on fixed mutants, resample users within category, retaining each user’s paired controls and fault cases together. One mutant per class cannot estimate variation across fault implementations; repeated users provide no mutant replication. [Clustered-inference guidance](https://cameron.econ.ucdavis.edu/research/Cameron_Miller_JHR_2015.pdf). For independent user-level Bernoulli outcomes, use Wilson or exact Clopper–Pearson intervals. Zero events gives a one-sided 95% upper bound 1−0.05^(1/n): 8.94% at n=32; zero misses implies sensitivity ≥91.06%. These bounds require independence and the eligible denominator; naive bootstrap intervals degenerate at zero. [Exact binomial intervals](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section2/prc241.htm).
